content: The Dietary Reference Intake (DRI) is a comprehensive system of nutritional recommendations established by the Institute of Medicine (IOM) of the United States National Academy. This system is utilized in both the United States and Canada and is designed to guide the general public as well as healthcare professionals. Its applications include use in food labeling, dietary planning for institutions such as schools, prisons, hospitals, and nursing homes, development of new food products by industries, and formulation of healthcare policies by public health officials. In 1997, the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) was incorporated into the broader and more detailed DRI system, as suggested by the Institute of Medicine. The RDA, originally developed during World War II by Lydia J. Roberts, Hazel K. Stiebeling, and Helen S. Mitchell under the National Academy of Sciences, was created to address nutritional issues that could impact national defense. The Food and Nutrition Board, established in 1941, began formulating recommendations for daily nutrient allowances to support the nutritional needs of the armed forces, civilians, and populations requiring food relief overseas. The initial guidelines, which included allowances for energy and eight essential nutrients, were reviewed by experts and finalized as the RDAs in 1941. These allowances were designed to ensure optimal nutrition for both civilians and military personnel, incorporating a margin of safety to account for variability in individual needs. During wartime food rationing, government-issued food guides also considered food availability when advising citizens on their nutritional intake. The Food and Nutrition Board has since revised the RDAs every five to ten years. In the early 1950s, USDA nutritionists introduced a new set of guidelines that included recommended servings of each food group, making it easier for individuals to meet their RDAs for essential nutrients. The current DRI recommendations consist of the following components: 1. Estimated Average Requirements (EAR): This represents the nutrient intake level expected to meet the needs of 50% of individuals in a specific age and gender group. 2. Reference Daily Intake (RDI): This is the daily dietary intake level of a nutrient considered sufficient to meet the requirements of nearly all (97–98%) healthy individuals in each life stage and gender group. 3. Adequate Intake (AI): When an RDI cannot be established, AI is used as a guideline. It represents an intake level believed to be adequate for everyone in the demographic group, though it is based on less robust evidence. 4. Tolerable Upper Intake Levels (UL): These are established to caution against excessive intake of nutrients, such as vitamin D, which can be harmful in large amounts. For vitamins and minerals, RDIs, AIs, and ULs are specified for different demographic groups, including age, gender, pregnant women, lactating women, and breastfeeding infants. For example, ULs marked as ND (not determined) indicate that a safe upper limit could not be established, and it is recommended that intake of these nutrients come from food sources only to avoid adverse effects. Additionally, certain substances are advised not to be added to food or dietary supplements due to inconclusive research on their potential adverse effects. For macronutrients, specific RDIs and AIs are provided for males aged 19–30 years, with variations for other age and gender groups.
